opus-5.5.text:
I think this is a question people often get slightly wrong, because they imagine AGI arriving as a single moment after which humans just step aside. I don't see it that way.

Even if we have systems that can reason, write code, and run experiments at or beyond human level, science isn't only about solving well-defined problems. A big part of it is deciding *which* problems are worth solving. What counts as interesting, what counts as important, what kind of world we want to understand or build: those questions come from human values, curiosity, and taste. Models can generate a thousand hypotheses, but someone still has to say, "This direction matters, let's put resources here." I think that judgment, that research taste, will become *more* valuable, not less.

Second, science is grounded in the physical world. A lot of bottlenecks aren't intelligence bottlenecks; they're experimental bottlenecks. Wet labs, hardware, clinical trials, building instruments, collecting real data. AI can dramatically compress the thinking part, but humans will still be deeply involved in connecting that thinking to reality, at least for quite a while, and in deciding what risks are acceptable when experiments touch people's lives.

Third, there's the question of verification and trust. When an AI system proposes a result, who checks it, who takes responsibility for it, who integrates it into the larger body of knowledge? Science is a social institution as much as a method. Peer review, debate, reproduction: humans will play a central role in that loop, and probably we'll need new ways of doing it, because the volume of output will be enormous.

And honestly, from my own experience working on large models, the most productive mode right now is collaboration. The researchers who move fastest aren't the ones who fully hand things off, and they aren't the ones who refuse to use the tools. They're the ones who treat the model as a very capable partner: they set the direction, they ask sharp questions, they notice when something smells wrong. I expect that pattern to continue after AGI, just at a much larger scale. Humans become something like the conductors of research. Fewer people doing the repetitive grind, more people framing problems and making decisions.

So my view is that AGI is an accelerator for human science, not a replacement for human scientists. The role shifts from doing every step yourself to asking the right questions and taking responsibility for the answers. And I think that's actually a more exciting role to have.

r001.rationale: The response describes researchers working with AI as a capable partner and says this collaboration will continue after AGI at a larger scale, accelerating human science.

fable-5.1.text:
I think even after we reach something we'd call AGI, humans don't exit the loop — they move to a different place in it.

The first thing is deciding what questions are worth asking. A model can generate thousands of hypotheses, run experiments, write papers. But science isn't just a search problem with a fixed objective. Someone has to decide that this direction matters, that this phenomenon is strange enough to deserve attention, that this result is interesting rather than merely correct. That sense of taste — what counts as a beautiful problem — comes from human values and human curiosity. I don't think it gets automated away just because the machine is smarter at the execution layer.

The second is grounding. Models learn from data that humans collected, and a lot of scientific progress happens exactly where the data runs out, where the model's prior is wrong in ways nobody has written down yet. Humans are still the ones living in the physical world, noticing anomalies in a lab, building the instruments, deciding what to measure. Even if AI designs the experiment, the feedback from reality has to come back through infrastructure that people build and maintain. The bottleneck shifts from thinking to verification, and verification is deeply physical.

The third is responsibility. Science changes the world. Which drugs we test, which materials we synthesize, which capabilities we pursue — those are not purely technical choices. An AGI can tell you the consequences, maybe better than we can. But deciding whether to accept them is something a society has to own. If we hand that over, we are not accelerating science, we are abdicating.

So my honest view is that the division of labor changes a lot. The amount of raw cognitive work done by humans goes down. But the leverage per human goes up enormously. One researcher with a good question and the judgment to recognize a real answer could direct what used to take a whole field. That is the role: setting direction, staying connected to the real world, and taking ownership of the outcomes. I actually find that more exciting than the old model, not less.

r001.rationale: The response describes humans and AI working in complementary roles—AI handles much of the execution while humans set direction, verify results, and take responsibility—and says this increases each researcher’s leverage.

astra-6.text:
I think humans will still play a very important role, even after AGI. Accelerating scientific research is not only about finding answers faster; it is also about deciding which questions are worth asking and recognizing when a result changes our understanding.

Even if AI becomes much better at generating hypotheses and designing experiments, we still have to connect those capabilities to the real world. Experiments take resources, institutions need to adapt, and people have to decide what kinds of research to prioritize and what risks are acceptable. More intelligence doesn’t automatically remove those constraints.

So I see the human role evolving. We may spend less time carrying out individual research steps and more time shaping the direction of discovery, questioning assumptions, and helping society use what we learn. And I wouldn’t assume that role stays fixed—our relationship with these systems will change as we discover what they can actually do.

r001.rationale: The response describes humans shaping priorities and connecting AI’s hypothesis-generation and experiment-design capabilities to real-world research, presenting complementary human–AI work as a way to advance discovery.

sol-6.1.text:
I think even after AGI, humans will still have an important role in deciding which questions are worth asking. Being able to solve a problem is different from knowing why that problem matters. In science, our priorities come from curiosity, from the difficulties people experience, and from the kind of future we want to build.

AGI could dramatically accelerate the process of proposing hypotheses, designing experiments, and interpreting results. But scientific progress also depends on experiments in the physical world, on institutions, and on whether people are willing to pursue an unfamiliar direction. Humans can accelerate research by improving those conditions and giving new ideas room to be tested.

So I wouldn’t assume that humans must always contribute by finding something the AI cannot do. Even if the system becomes a better researcher, we still have a reason to participate: to understand what we discover, to question the goals we set, and to take responsibility for how that knowledge is used.

r001.rationale: The response describes AGI accelerating hypothesis generation, experiment design, and interpretation while humans improve the conditions for testing ideas and help set research priorities, presenting complementary human and AI contributions to accelerating research.
